question.prompt: Given that \(i^2=-1,\) for how many integers \(n\) is \((n+i)^4\) an integer?

solutions.explanation:
An integer must have zero imaginary part. Squaring twice lets us find that part using only \(i^2=-1\). First,
\[
(n+i)^2=(n^2-1)+2ni.
\]
Squaring again gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(n+i)^4
&=(n^2-1)^2-4n^2+4n(n^2-1)i\\
&=n^4-6n^2+1+4n(n^2-1)i.
\end{aligned}
\]
For integer \(n\), the real part \(n^4-6n^2+1\) is already an integer. Therefore the whole expression is an integer exactly when
\[
4n(n^2-1)=4n(n-1)(n+1)=0.
\]
A product is zero only if one of its factors is zero, so the complete list is \(n=-1,0,1\). These give the integer values \(-4,1,-4\), respectively. Thus exactly \(3\) integers \(n\) work, choice D.
solutions.title: Separate the real and imaginary parts
